newsitem.title: USA: W.House sorry stock manipulator invited to coffee.
newsitem.headline: W.House sorry stock manipulator invited to coffee.

text.p: The White House said on Saturday that it was unfortunate that a New Jersey stock promoter, convicted of criminal securities fraud that benefited an organised crime family, was invited to a coffee meeting with President Bill Clinton in December 1995.

A White House spokesman, Lanny Davis, commenting on the case of Eric Wynn, said: "Based on the facts and circumstances as we understand them, Mr. Wynn was not an appropriate person to be included at a White House event such as this."

Davis commented in reaction to a Washington Post report that said Wynn was among eight guests who accepted an invitation to join Clinton and top Democratic Party leaders for an early morning coffee meeting four days before Christmas 1995.

It said he bilked millions from investors and had already served two years in prison after a 1989 guilty plea on theft and tax charges. It said Wynn's stock manipulation had benefited a member of the Bonanno organised crime family. Administration officials said Wynn was invited to the event by the Democratic National Committee.
Davis said the White House is working to bring in new procedures to screen more closely the people who are invited to attend White House events.

"As the president has stated, he believes previous policies regarding vetting of White House guests were lax. He has instructed the White House counsel and staff to institute new procedures and such evaluation of these procedures is ongoing at the present time," Davis said.

An unidentified close associate of Wynn's quoted in the Post said Wynn was trying to obtain a pardon for his July 21, 1995, stock manipulation conviction, but that the Justice Department had no record of any formal request by Wynn for a pardon.
The Post said Wynn was brought into Democratic fund-raising circles by Richard Mays, an Arkansas lawyer who served as a Clinton appointee on the Arkansas Supreme Court in the early 1980s.

Wynn's second conviction occurred five months before the Dec. 21, 1995, coffee meeting with Clinton. He was sentenced in September to 52 months in prison and ordered to pay a $50,000 fine. Wynn is free on bail while appealing the conviction, the Post said.

The White House has been embarrassed by disclosures that guests at functions over the past four years have included a convicted drug dealer and the head of a Chinese arms company now under investigation by U.S. authorities.
Questions have arisen about Clinton's White House coffee chats with wealthy people, many of whom later contributed large sums to the Democrats -- a reported total of $27 million.

Clinton has insisted no laws were broken in the way Democrats attracted donors. But there have been so many questions raised that Republicans in Congress are promising oversight hearings and want Clinton to appoint an independent counsel to investigate.
